question: What is EV/ARR, and how does the Rule of 40 affect the multiple a software company deserves?
model_answer_md:
**ARR** is annual recurring revenue — the subscription base, stripped of one-off implementation and services income. EV/ARR prices that base, and it is the working multiple in software because most of these companies have no meaningful EBITDA.

The **Rule of 40** says revenue growth plus free cash flow margin should clear roughly 40. A company growing 50 % while burning 20 % of revenue scores 30; one growing 20 % at a 25 % margin scores 45.

It matters because it prices the trade-off software companies constantly make. Growth bought by burning cash is worth less than growth that funds itself — and a company below 40 is spending more to grow than the growth is returning.

So the multiple is not read off a flat median. Analysts plot EV/ARR against growth, or against the Rule of 40 score, and read the target off that line at its own numbers.
key_points: ARR = the recurring subscription base, excluding one-off services revenue
EV/ARR is standard because most software companies have no useful EBITDA
Rule of 40 = growth % + FCF margin %, with 40 as the rough pass mark
It prices the trade-off between growth and cash burn
Read the multiple off a line against growth, not from a flat median

follow_ups.question: Two companies both score 30 on the Rule of 40. Do they deserve the same multiple?
follow_ups.answer_md: Not necessarily. A company growing 50 % with a −20 % margin has a different future from one growing 10 % with a +20 % margin, even at the same score. High growth with burn can still compound into a much larger business if the unit economics work; slow growth with modest cash generation is closer to a mature company. The market generally pays more for the growth, provided the burn is funded and the payback on customer acquisition is short.

follow_ups.question: Where does net revenue retention come in?
follow_ups.answer_md: It is arguably the single best quality signal. Retention above 100 % means the existing customer base grows on its own through upsell and expansion, even before any new customers are won. A company at 120 % net retention has a fundamentally different growth cost from one at 95 %, and it usually earns a premium multiple for it.

weak_answer_note: Defines the Rule of 40 as a formula without saying what trade-off it captures, or treats it as a pass/fail test rather than one input into where on the line a company sits.
